Let [latex]c_{1}....c_{n}[/latex] be scalars, not all zero, such that [latex]\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}a_{i}=0[/latex]
where [latex]a_{i}[/latex] are column vectors in [latex]R^{n}[/latex]. Consider the set of linear equations Ax = b
where A=[latex]a_{1}....a_{n}[/latex] and b=[latex]\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}[/latex]. The set of equations has
questions.solution:
[latex]\sum c_ia_i=0[/latex] with not all [latex]c_i[/latex] zero means the columns are dependent, so Ax = 0 has a non-zero solution c.

[latex]x=(1,\ldots,1)[/latex] solves Ax = b, and so does [latex](1,\ldots,1)+tc[/latex] for every t [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] infinitely many solutions.

Answer: infinitely many solutions

questions.solution:
Multiply top and bottom by [latex]\sqrt{1+x}+\sqrt{1-x}[/latex]:
[latex]\frac{(1+x)-(1-x)}{x(\sqrt{1+x}+\sqrt{1-x})}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+x}+\sqrt{1-x}}\rightarrow\frac22=1[/latex]

Answer: 1

questions.text:
What is the sum to infinity of the series,
[latex]3+6 x^{2}+9 x^{4}+12 x^{6}+\ldots \text { given }|x| \lt 1[/latex]
questions.solution:
Let [latex]y=x^2[/latex]. The series is [latex]3(1+2y+3y^2+\cdots)=\frac{3}{(1-y)^2}[/latex] (since [latex]\sum (k+1)y^k=\frac{1}{(1-y)^2}[/latex]).

Sum [latex]=\frac{3}{(1-x^2)^2}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\frac{3}{(1-x^2)^2}[/latex]

questions.text: The value of the expression [latex]13^{99}[/latex](mod 17), in the range 0 to 16, is _________.
questions.solution:
[latex]13\equiv-4\pmod{17}[/latex], so [latex]13^2\equiv16\equiv-1[/latex] and [latex]13^4\equiv1[/latex].

[latex]99=4\times24+3\Rightarrow13^{99}\equiv13^3=13^2\cdot13\equiv-13\equiv4\pmod{17}[/latex]

Answer: 4
